extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent prosecutors, in-house counsel, and judges involved in patent infringement disputes
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedures for construing disputed patent claim terms in a Markman (claim construction) hearing in U.S. patent litigation, including the evidence to consider, procedural steps, and governing case law and PTO rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of a Markman hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markman hearing (claim construction hearing) is held to determine the meaning of disputed claims in patent litigation; the judge, as the trier of law, will determine how the claims should be interpreted and that determination will be incorporated into the jury’s instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This hearing is essential because patent claims define what is and is not protected. Although the jury determines infringement (including under the doctrine of equivalents), the judge determines claim scope. The name comes from Markman v. Westview Instruments (1996).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary reliance on intrinsic evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts will consider intrinsic evidence first when conducting claim construction. Intrinsic evidence refers to materials submitted as part of the patent application: the patent application itself (claims, summary, written description), prosecution history (written or oral communications with the examiner), previous related patents and their prosecution history, and prior art referenced in the patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intrinsic evidence is given significant weight because it points to the applicant’s thought process. Claims must be read in view of the specification; specifications are the best guide and may contain special meanings or internal disclaimers. Prosecution history plays a role but may be ambiguous due to negotiation with the examiner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use extrinsic evidence only for background and education
rubrics_metrics.description: Extrinsic evidence includes dictionary definitions, encyclopedias/engineering dictionaries, journals or scientific treatises, testimony from the patent applicant, and expert testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extrinsic evidence is useful to educate the court and explain technology or what a person of ordinary skill in the art would understand at the effective filing date. However, it should not be substituted for intrinsic evidence and carries the risk of altering claim meaning or expanding scope if misapplied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary meaning to a person of ordinary skill in the art (Phillips)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Phillips v. AWH Corp., each claim term must be given 'the meaning that the term would have to a person of ordinary skill in the art in question at the time of the invention' (the effective filing date); that meaning is the 'ordinary meaning' baseline for claim construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ordinary meaning is an objective baseline but may not always be the proper construction if intrinsic evidence shows a different meaning. Timing is important—use materials contemporaneous with the effective filing date to determine the level of skill and meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read claims in view of the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be read in view of the specification; specifications are highly relevant and are the best guide to the meaning of a disputed term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifications may define special meanings for terms or contain internal disclaimers that govern construction. Reliance on the specification is a central part of intrinsic-evidence-based analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution history and disclaimers affect claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments and statements made during prosecution (prosecution history) can result in disclaimers and influence how courts interpret claim language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will consider prosecution history to the extent it clarifies what the applicant disclaimed or amended, but prosecution history sometimes lacks clarity because it reflects negotiation with the examiner and may be more ambiguous than the application or grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extrinsic evidence cannot override intrinsic evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Although courts generally permit extrinsic evidence, it should not be used as a substitute for a careful reading of the claims and the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because extrinsic sources are not written with the particular patent in mind, there is a risk they could be used improperly to change claim meaning; courts therefore treat extrinsic evidence as secondary and for background only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contemporaneous technical literature to assess ordinary skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Extrinsic sources (treatises, journals) from the time of filing are useful to understand what a person of ordinary skill in the art would have known at that time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because technology advances quickly, using sources from the relevant time frame (effective filing date) is important—for example, a treatise from the time the patent was filed better reflects the relevant level of skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct minor mistakes in claim language; major corrections require PTO
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may correct minor mistakes and typos in claim language where there is no reasonable debate as to the correction, but major errors generally must be corrected by the Patent Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correction is permitted only where the proper correction is obvious and undisputed; otherwise, the Patent Office must address substantive changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer claim interpretation that preserves validity when interpretations are equally plausible
rubrics_metrics.description: The Phillips court indicated claims should be construed in a way that preserves patent validity when two equally viable interpretations exist, choosing the one that preserves validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle typically applies only when the intrinsic record supports two equally reasonable constructions—courts will favor the construction that keeps the patent valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO claim construction rule (37 CFR 42.100) aligns certain proceedings with Phillips
rubrics_metrics.description: As of November 2018, the USPTO adopted 37 CFR 42.100 to bring claim construction rules for IPR, PGR, and CBM proceedings in line with Phillips; prior civil or ITC claim construction decisions properly entered into the record may be considered by the PTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule applies to petitions filed after its adoption; it replaces the broadest-reasonable-interpretation (BRI) standard for those proceedings but BRI remains for petitions filed earlier and for reexaminations and reissues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) standard (historical PTO standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the old BRI standard the PTO gave claims their broadest possible interpretation and required challengers to show the claim was being interpreted more broadly than a court would; claimed words were given their ordinary and customary meaning unless the applicant defined terms in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BRI tended to increase the possibility that claims would be interpreted to encompass prior art and thus be cancelled. Extrinsic evidence could be considered but intrinsic evidence was favored even under BRI. BRI remains applicable for some earlier-filed proceedings and reexaminations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local rules and judge discretion control timing and procedure of Markman hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: There is little uniform guidance on when Markman hearings should be held; timing varies by district and judge and is governed by local patent rules consistent with the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some districts hold hearings early (e.g., Northern District of California), others as an intermediate step or near trial. Courts may decide a hearing is unnecessary based on submitted papers. Procedures may be modified per case complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meet-and-confer and narrowing disputed terms to streamline hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts typically require parties to meet and confer to determine which claims are actually in dispute; if parties agree on constructions, the hearing may be unnecessary or may focus only on disputed terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying and stipulating to constructions can save time and money; some courts request a specific identification of disputed claims to streamline proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction discovery and briefing requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties engage in claim construction discovery, exchanging documentation relevant to their arguments, and typically prepare claim construction briefs outlining their positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent holders may need to provide internal memoranda; expert witnesses are often used. Briefs frequently include images or graphics to illustrate the inventions because of technical material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of tech tutorials and multimedia to educate the court
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may submit a 'tech tutorial' to educate the court on the relevant technology; this can be live presentations (attorneys or experts) or videos with graphics and narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some judges hold the tutorial before the Markman hearing, others combine them. Use depends on the technology and the judge’s familiarity; tutorials are optional and intended to aid understanding, not substitute for claim analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment of special masters or technical advisors when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges may appoint patent special masters to oversee claim construction proceedings or technical advisors to assist with technical vocabulary and theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special masters may be used in complex technology fields or heavy caseloads. Technical advisors must be appointed via a fair and open procedure and, like judges, may not engage in ex parte communications with either party.
